options: Marks a function as a test so `cargo test` discovers and runs it
Makes a function run automatically at program startup
Tells the compiler to optimize the function more aggressively
Marks a function as deprecated
quiz.explain: `#[test]` is what `cargo test` looks for. A function without it is treated as ordinary code and never gets run as a test.

quiz.q: Which macro fails the test when its two arguments are equal?
options: assert!
assert_eq!
assert_ne!
assert_panic!
quiz.explain: `assert_ne!(a, b)` panics (failing the test) if `a` and `b` ARE equal — the 'these must differ' check.

quiz.q: What does `#[cfg(test)]` on `mod tests` actually do?
options: It hides the module's compile warnings
It compiles the module only when running `cargo test`, so it's absent from release builds entirely
It runs the tests in a separate thread
It disables the tests without deleting them
quiz.explain: `#[cfg(test)]` is a compile-time switch: in a normal `cargo build`, that module isn't compiled at all, so it adds zero size or dependencies to your shipped binary.

quiz.q: Inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }`, what does `use super::*;` do?
options: Imports every crate in the Cargo registry
Brings items from the parent module (including private ones) into scope
Runs all tests in the parent module first
Marks the module as a superset of another module
quiz.explain: `super` refers to the enclosing module. `use super::*` pulls in everything defined there, including private functions — this is why unit tests can reach private internals.

options: There is no difference, `expected` is just documentation
`expected` makes the test run faster
Plain `#[should_panic]` passes on any panic; `expected` also checks the panic message contains that substring
`expected` disables the panic check entirely
quiz.explain: Without `expected`, the test passes if the code panics for ANY reason, even an unrelated bug. Adding `expected = "..."` verifies the panic message actually matches, so you know you're panicking for the right reason.

quiz.q: How do you run only the tests whose name contains "parse"?
options: cargo test --only parse
cargo test parse
cargo run --test parse
cargo test --filter=parse
quiz.explain: `cargo test <substring>` runs only tests whose full path (module + function name) contains that substring.

quiz.q: A `#[test]` function has no `assert!`/`assert_eq!`/`assert_ne!` calls at all. What happens when you run it?
options: It fails to compile
It always fails
It always passes, because nothing inside it can fail
cargo test skips it with a warning
quiz.explain: A test with no assertion has nothing that can panic, so it always passes — and checks absolutely nothing. Every real test needs at least one assertion.

quiz.q: Why doesn't `#[cfg(test)]` test code increase the size of your shipped release binary?
options: The linker strips it out after compiling
Rust compresses test code separately
It's never compiled in the first place outside of `cargo test`
Test code is stored in a separate file automatically
quiz.explain: `#[cfg(test)]` is evaluated at compile time — the annotated module simply isn't part of the source the compiler processes for a normal `cargo build`, so it can't contribute to binary size.

flashcards.front: What three things does every test need?
flashcards.back: A `#[test]` attribute, at least one assertion, and a descriptive name so a failure tells you what broke.
`assert!(cond)` fails if cond is false. `assert_eq!(a, b)` fails if a != b (and prints both values). `assert_ne!(a, b)` fails if a == b.

flashcards.front: Where do unit tests conventionally live, and why?
flashcards.back: In a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; ... }` block in the same file as the code — `use super::*` gives access to private items, and `#[cfg(test)]` excludes the whole module from non-test builds.

flashcards.front: What does `#[cfg(test)]` guarantee that just 'not calling the function' doesn't?
flashcards.back: It's a compile-time exclusion — the module isn't compiled at all outside `cargo test`, so it can safely use dev-dependencies and adds zero size to release builds.

flashcards.front: When should you use `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]` instead of plain `#[should_panic]`?
flashcards.back: Whenever you want to make sure the code panicked for the RIGHT reason. Plain `#[should_panic]` passes on any panic, even from an unrelated bug.

flashcards.front: How do you run just one test, or a group of tests matching a name?
flashcards.back: `cargo test <substring>` — it matches against the full test path (module::function_name).

flashcards.front: Why is a test with no assertions dangerous?
flashcards.back: It always passes, giving false confidence — it looks like coverage but checks nothing.

flashcards.front: What convention does `assert_eq!(a, b)` follow, and what happens if you swap the order?
flashcards.back: Convention is `assert_eq!(actual, expected)`. Swapping still works correctly (it still fails on mismatch), it just flips which value the panic message labels 'left' vs 'right'.
